Only a thin sliver at the far right, the last 17 months from May 2005, is marked as the real guarantee.

3. Today's guarantee, probably a product or protection promising a floor or outcome, has only existed in real life for 17 months. The long track record people see, 856 start months going back to 1934, is a simulation applied retroactively, not actual history. So the guarantee has almost no real-world track record, and most of the apparent evidence for it is hypothetical.

4. A viewer would take away caution. Do not treat the long backtested results as proof of how the product performs. It has almost no real track record, so judge it on its terms, cost and the issuer's ability to pay, not on the what-if history. As a 40-something with 20 years to invest, this suggests not shifting out of cash or T-bills into a guaranteed product just because the backtest looks good.

1. The animation sets up a comparison between two ways of holding money for 20 years: rolling over 3-month Treasury bills one after another (80 bills in total), versus a savings bond that is guaranteed to double (x2) by year 20. It ends by asking "Which path ends with more?"

In frames 4 to 6, the savings bond bar is added above it, labeled "guaranteed" with a x2 marker at year 20, and it fills from partway across to the full length. The 80-bill row sits beneath it. Both paths end at year 20, and the closing frame poses the question. All frames are marked "illustrative".

3. It means that repeatedly rolling short-term T-bills means reinvesting 80 times at whatever rates prevail each time, so the final result is uncertain. The bond offers a known, locked-in doubling at year 20. The point is to compare an uncertain rolled-over outcome with a guaranteed one over the same horizon. The frames do not show which ends higher, since the question is left open.

4. The viewer would likely take away that money not needed for 20 years does not have to sit in cash or short-term bills. They should weigh the guaranteed long-term doubling of a savings bond against the uncertain result of rolling T-bills, and consider whether the bond fits their goal. The animation does not give a firm verdict, and the "illustrative" label means the numbers are not a forecast.
9ea26855:
1. The animation shows a hypothetical "guarantee": money that is guaranteed to double (x2) over 20 years, and asks whether that doubling actually keeps up with rising prices. The label "IF today's guarantee had existed" shows it is a what-if built from historical periods starting in Jan 1966, with the full set of 20-year start dates running from 1934 to 2006.

2. A solid white bar (the money after doubling) is compared with a dashed outline bar (what the original money could buy). In frames 1 to 3 the outline grows taller than the white bar, and a red sliver appears at its top. That sliver is the purchasing power the doubled money fails to cover. Frame 4 adds the text "x2 bought 58.0% of what the original bought" and starts drawing a timeline from 1934 to 2006. Frame 5 shows the whole timeline: grey areas where the money kept up with prices, and a large red area where it fell behind. Frame 6 adds the summary "58.7% of starts kept up".

3. Doubling your money over 20 years is not safe in real terms. Prices rose enough in the 1966 case that the doubled money bought only about 58% of what the original bought. Across all the 20-year starting points, the doubling kept up with prices only about 58.7% of the time. In the other roughly 41% of cases, especially for starts in the 1950s to 1970s, it lost purchasing power, shown by the red area. A fixed nominal gain, like what cash or short-term Treasuries earn, can quietly lose real value.

4. A viewer in their 40s with money they will not need for about 20 years would conclude that a nominal "guaranteed" return is not the same as safety. Holding it in a bank account or T-bills risks losing purchasing power, and over a 20-year horizon they should consider assets that have historically beaten inflation, such as stocks or inflation-protected bonds (TIPS). The animation does not say which to choose or how much to hold, and it does not show how stocks or other assets did. It only argues that nominal doubling can fall short of keeping up with prices.
